Eastern parts of the Old World, from India (Mumbai) to Fiji, and from 46° N in northern China to Australia (New South Wales) and Lord Howe Island at 32° S, and in the New World from North America (Washington State) to South America (southern Brazil)
In Peninsular Malaysia, 21 species of which 3 (Symplocos calycactylos, S. nivea and S. pyriflora) are endemic
Symplocos theifolia, recorded in Singapore, is also included in this account.
In temperate and tropical regions, in the tropics most abundant in mountains, to c. 4000 m on G. Kinabalu and the New Guinea mountains, where it is represented by microphyllous dwarf shrubs
Everywhere a constituent of mixed, mostly evergreen rain forest, not in arid zones.

Some species of Symplocos accumulate aluminium and their bark and leaves have been used as a yellow dye for batik cloth or woven pandan and rattan or as a mordant for the red dye from Morinda but in Peninsular Malaysia chemical dyes are now used
Aluminium accumulation is associated with leaves that dry yellow-green and with blue fruits that are found in this genus (Mabberley, 2008).
Ridley (1923) following Moritzi (1848) recognised Cordyloblaste as a separate genus
It is here treated as a subgenus with two species (Symplocos henschelii and S. pendula), the remaining 20 species fall within subgen. Symplocos
Due to the occurrence of species complexes, sometimes subspecies and varieties are recognised
